_note: Thuso Points. What a household earns for looking after itself, and a separate, deliberately non-monetary track for nurses. Read directly by apps/web; generated into Swift and Kotlin by scripts/emit-rewards.mjs. Money is not described here — packages/catalog/earnings.json owns every rand a nurse is paid and this file may not name one. What a point is worth is stated once, in `randPerPoint`, and every screen on every platform multiplies rather than restates it.
_lawNote: Section 18A of the Medicines and Related Substances Act 101 of 1965: no person shall supply any medicine according to a bonus system, rebate system or any other incentive scheme. That single sentence is why this contract can only ever touch packages/catalog/shop.json, which sells no medicine, and why `medicineEarnsNothing` is enforced by arithmetic in packages/commerce rather than written down as an intention. The same section is why there is no point in this file for collecting a script, for finishing a course, or for taking a dose — an adherence reward is an incentive scheme attached to a medicine no matter which screen it is drawn on.
_popiaNote: A points ledger is not a clinical record and must never become one by accident. Health data is special personal information under POPIA; the fact that a person attended a visit on a date is ordinary personal information, but the reason for that visit is not. Every earning reason below therefore carries `discloses`, and packages/commerce refuses to write a ledger line that carries anything else. A ledger row reads 'a booked visit was attended' and never which visit or what for.
_randPerPointNote: Ten points to the rand, in one place. A screen that wants to show what a balance is worth multiplies by this; a screen that hard-codes 'R10' has created a second copy of a number that will be wrong the day this one changes.

earnReasons.never: the patient, the address, or the clinical content

earnReasons.never: which checks, or anything about a check that failed

_tierNote: Tiers are earned on points in the last twelve months and buy convenience — never care, never a price on a medicine, and never a place in a clinical queue. The inputs are listed exhaustively in `tierInputs` and checked, because a tier quietly influenced by where somebody lives is redlining with a friendly name.
tierInputs: points earned in the last 12 months

tiers.name: Green
tiers.benefit: Points on everything the shop sells that is not a medicine, which is everything the shop sells.

tiers.name: Amber
tiers.benefit: Delivery at no charge on any order, whatever it comes to.

tiers.name: Deep green
tiers.benefit: Delivery at no charge, and the booking calendar opens a day earlier for routine visits.

refusals.sentence: Points are not money. They cannot be withdrawn, sent to anyone, or paid into a bank account.
refusals.why: A balance that can be cashed out is a deposit, and taking deposits is a licensed activity. It would also make every screen that awards a point a screen that hands out money, which is a very different thing to get wrong.

refusals.sentence: No medicine earns points, and no points come off the price of a medicine.
refusals.why: Section 18A of the Medicines and Related Substances Act 101 of 1965 prohibits supplying medicine under a bonus, rebate or incentive scheme. This is enforced by arithmetic in packages/commerce — a medicine earns zero and redeems zero — rather than by the shop merely happening not to stock one.

refusals.sentence: There are no points for taking your medicine, collecting a script, or finishing a course.
refusals.why: Paying somebody to take a drug is an incentive scheme attached to a medicine, and it pressures the person least able to argue — the one who is ill. Whether a dose was taken is also exactly the kind of detail this ledger must never hold.

refusals.sentence: Your points history shows that a visit happened. It never shows what it was for.
refusals.why: The reason for a visit is special personal information under POPIA. A points ledger is read casually, shown to family, screenshotted and pasted into chats — it is the worst possible container for a diagnosis.

refusals.sentence: A tier changes when you can book, never how quickly you are seen. Nobody is treated sooner for having more points.
refusals.why: The moment a balance moves a person up a clinical queue, care is being sold by loyalty rather than given by need, and the people with the fewest points are the ones who can least afford to wait.

refusals.sentence: Nothing about who you are affects your tier — only the points you have earned.
refusals.why: A protected category is never an input here, for the same reason it is never a header chip anywhere else in this product. A tier influenced by an area code is a tier influenced by race in this country's geography.

refusals.sentence: Recognition points are not pay, and they change nothing about what you are owed or which visits you are offered.
refusals.why: A nurse's income is settled entirely by packages/catalog/earnings.json. A second scoreboard that quietly affected dispatch would be a productivity target wearing a badge, and the thing it would squeeze is time spent with a patient.

refusals.sentence: If your tier drops, the points you have already earned stay yours.
refusals.why: The same principle as a suspension never touching money already earned. A balance that can be taken back is a promise the holder cannot rely on, and a person planning around it is being misled.

refusals.sentence: Points last 18 months. We tell you 60 days before any of them expire, and we tell you how many.
refusals.why: Silent expiry is how a loyalty scheme takes back what it advertised. The warning is part of the contract, not a courtesy, so both numbers live here and no screen may invent its own.

refusals.sentence: An account belonging to someone under eighteen does not earn or spend points. A guardian's account does.
refusals.why: A minor may hold a health record here under a guardian. Letting that record earn a spendable balance would make a child the target of an incentive scheme.
